title: Average Collection Period: Formula, Calculation & Examples
summary: Learn the average collection period formula with annual and monthly examples, how it compares to DSO, B2B benchmarks and how to shorten it.
body_markdown:
Average collection period is a key financial metric that shows how long it takes for your business to collect payments from customers after a credit sale. It’s calculated by dividing your average accounts receivable by your net credit sales, then multiplying by the number of days in the period. The result gives you a clear, time-based view of how efficiently your accounts receivable are managed and how quickly revenue turns into cash.


Understanding your average collection period helps you spot payment delays, evaluate your credit policies and improve your overall cash flow. Tracked consistently, it also shows trends in customer behavior, so you can act early and keep your collections process efficient and predictable. Keep reading to find out:

## What is Average Collection Period?


The average collection period is a financial metric that measures the average number of days it takes for a business to collect payments from customers after a credit sale. It shows how long your accounts receivable remain outstanding before being converted into cash.


This metric plays an important role in understanding your cash flow cycle and evaluating how efficiently your business manages collections. A shorter average collection period generally means customers are paying on time and your collections process is working. A longer period may point to payment delays, lenient credit terms or inefficiencies in your receivables process.


By tracking your average collection period over time, you can spot trends in customer payment behavior and act early to improve how quickly your business gets paid.


### Average Collection Period vs AR Turnover vs DSO


The average collection period,[accounts receivable turnover](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/accounts-receivable-turnover-ratio) and days sales outstanding (DSO) all measure how efficiently a business collects payments, but each presents the information differently.


Metric What it measures Formula Best used for


Average collection period Average number of days to collect payment after a credit sale (Average AR ÷ Net credit sales) × Number of days Assessing collection efficiency over a full period, such as a year


AR turnover Number of times receivables are collected during a period Net credit sales ÷ Average AR Comparing collection efficiency as a ratio in financial analysis


DSO Number of days of sales currently tied up in receivables (Ending AR ÷ Credit sales) × Number of days Monthly reporting and tracking trends over time


The average collection period and AR turnover are two views of the same calculation. Dividing 365 by your AR turnover ratio gives you your average collection period, so as turnover increases, your collection period decreases.


DSO is the metric most finance teams report month to month. The main difference is the receivables figure: the average collection period uses **average** accounts receivable across the period, while the simple[DSO formula](https://upflow.io/blog/reduce-dso/dso-calculation-formula) uses the **ending** balance. When receivables are stable, the two give similar results. When AR grows or shrinks sharply during the period, they can differ, and DSO reacts faster to recent changes. Some teams also call this measure[days sales in accounts receivable](https://upflow.io/blog/reduce-dso/days-sales-in-accounts-receivable) .


Using these metrics together gives you a more complete view of your collections performance: the average collection period and DSO give a time-based measure in days, while the turnover ratio shows efficiency as a ratio.


## Average Collection Period Formula


The average collection period calculates how long it takes, on average, for your business to collect payment after a credit sale. It’s expressed in days, which makes it easy to see how quickly cash is coming in.


The standard formula is:


Here it is as text, so you can copy it:


Average Collection Period = (Average Accounts Receivable ÷ Net Credit Sales) × Number of Days


Average accounts receivable is calculated by adding your beginning and ending[accounts receivable](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/accounts-receivable-management) balances for the period and dividing by two.[Net credit sales](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/net-credit-sales) include all sales made on credit, excluding returns and allowances. For the number of days, use 365 for a year, 90 for a quarter, or the number of days in the month for monthly figures.


This version of the formula gives you a direct view of how your receivables relate to your sales, translated into the number of days it takes to collect payment.


There’s also a simpler way to calculate the average collection period if you already know your AR turnover ratio:


Or, as text:


Average Collection Period = 365 ÷ Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio


This version converts the turnover ratio into days, which makes your collections performance easier to interpret. A lower number of days means faster collections, while a higher number means it takes longer to get paid.

## Average Collection Period Example


To see how the average collection period works in practice, let’s walk through a simple example.


Assume your business generated $100,000 in net credit sales over the year. Your accounts receivable balance was $8,000 at the beginning of the year and $12,000 at the end.


First, calculate your average accounts receivable:


($8,000 + $12,000) ÷ 2 = $10,000


Next, apply the formula:


($10,000 ÷ $100,000) × 365 = 36.5 days


Your average collection period is 36.5 days. In other words, it takes your business about 36.5 days on average to collect payment from customers after a credit sale.


You can also reach the same result using the accounts receivable turnover ratio. Your turnover ratio is $100,000 ÷ $10,000 = 10, and dividing 365 by 10 gives you the same 36.5 days.


### How to Calculate the Average Collection Period for a Month


The same formula works for a single month. Just use that month’s figures and the number of days in it.


Say your net credit sales for March were $9,000. Your accounts receivable was $11,000 at the start of March and $13,000 at the end:


- Average accounts receivable: ($11,000 + $13,000) ÷ 2 = $12,000
- Average collection period: ($12,000 ÷ $9,000) × 31 = 41.3 days


March’s 41.3 days is higher than the 36.5-day annual figure, which suggests collections slowed down that month. A quick look at your[AR aging report](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/aging-reports) will show which customers are behind the change. Tracking the metric monthly like this also gives you a more reliable base for[cash flow forecasting](https://upflow.io/blog/cfo-reads/cash-flow-forecasting) , since you can see slowdowns as they happen rather than at year-end.


Looking at the average collection period in this way gives you a clear, time-based view of how quickly your business converts receivables into cash.


## Importance of Average Collection Period


The average collection period shows how efficiently your business turns credit sales into cash. It affects your liquidity, your collections performance and your overall financial stability.


1. **Cash flow management:** A shorter collection period means cash comes in sooner, which supports stronger liquidity and reduces reliance on[invoice financing](https://upflow.io/blog/business-to-business-payments/invoice-financing) to cover gaps.
2. **Credit policy assessment:** The metric shows whether your credit terms are too strict or too lenient. A long collection period can point to relaxed terms or slow follow-up, while a short one reflects tight credit control.
3. **Customer payment behavior:** Tracking it over time highlights consistent delays and high-risk accounts, so you can adjust your[financial relationship](https://upflow.io/financial-relationship-management) strategy with each customer.
4. **Benchmarking:** Comparing your collection period with industry averages shows where you stand. Upflow’s research on[cash collection benchmarks](https://upflow.io/blog/business-to-business-payments/cash-collection-benchmarks-online-payments) shows how much collection speed varies across businesses.
5. **Forecasting and budgeting:** A predictable collection period makes cash inflows easier to plan, which improves your[cash flow](https://upflow.io/blog/cfo-reads/cash-flow-analysis) planning. It also gives your[cash forecasting](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/cash-forecasting-growing-companies) a realistic timing assumption for when receivables will turn into cash.


## What is a Good Average Collection Period?


A good average collection period is one that’s close to your agreed payment terms and compares well with your industry. In general, shorter is better, since it means you’re collecting efficiently and keeping cash flow strong.


As a rule of thumb, your average collection period should be close to your[payment terms](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/net-30-terms) . For example, if your terms are net 30, collecting within 30 to 45 days is typically considered healthy. If your collection period sits well above your terms, customers are paying late, whatever your industry.


What counts as good also varies widely by industry. To benchmark performance, many businesses look at median[DSO](https://upflow.io/blog/reduce-dso/calculate-dso) , a closely related metric. Our[State of B2B Payments 2024 report](https://upflow.io/blog/business-to-business-payments/b2b-payment-insights) shows how it varies across sectors:


The chart compares the median DSO in each industry with the top 25% of performers on Upflow. Here are the same figures as a table:

Across all industries, the overall median is 56 days. Traditional service industries like Office & Facilities Management and Consulting tend to have longer collection periods, often because longer payment terms are common in those sectors. Clothing, Accessories & Home businesses collect fastest, thanks to faster inventory cycles and stricter payment enforcement.


These differences come down to how businesses operate. Companies that sell physical goods can enforce payment more easily, for example by holding the next order until outstanding invoices are paid, while service businesses often find it harder to pause what they provide.


Ultimately, a good average collection period is one that aligns with your payment terms and compares favorably with your industry benchmarks.


## How to Improve Your Average Collection Period?


When your average collection period starts rising, the cause is usually in your own process rather than with your customers. Start by finding what’s driving the increase, then fix it at the source.


What's driving it What to do


Invoices sent late or with errors Invoice as soon as work is delivered, using a standard template


Invoices going to the wrong contact Confirm billing and AP contacts when you onboard each customer


No reminders before the due date Send automated reminders a few days before each invoice is due


Disputes left unresolved Give every dispute an owner and resolve it before it ages


Paying is inconvenient Offer online payment options and a payment link on every invoice


Credit terms too generous for risky accounts Review credit limits and terms based on payment history


A few large customers paying late Escalate early and involve the account owner from sales or customer success


Once you know where the delays come from, these five strategies will help you reduce your average collection period and get paid faster:


1. **Implement a consistent invoicing system:** Set clear, predictable billing schedules so customers know when and how they’ll be invoiced. That helps them plan their payments and reduces delays.
2. **Streamline invoices for clarity:** Make sure invoices are easy to read and clearly outline each charge. Clear invoices reduce confusion and help customers review and approve payments more quickly.
3. **Automate payment reminders:** Use automated, account-level[payment reminders](https://upflow.io/blog/payment-reminders/payment-reminders) to keep customers informed of outstanding balances, so it’s easier for them to pay on time. You can streamline this process with a[financial CRM](https://upflow.io/financial-relationship-management) like Upflow.
4. **Offer flexible payment options:** Provide several payment methods, including an[online payment system](https://upflow.io/blog/business-to-business-payments/online-payment-system) , so customers can pay as soon as they receive an invoice.
5. **Incentivize early payments:** Offer[early payment discounts](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/net-30-terms#early-payment-discounts-210-net-30-and-more) to encourage customers to settle invoices ahead of the due date.


Applying these strategies consistently will help shorten your average collection period, leading to improved[cash flow](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/cashflow-dashboard) and stronger financial stability.
